title: Star Wars: Galactic Racer 如何通过「分布式开发」保持核心团队精简与可持续
content:
How Star Wars: Galactic Racer kept the core team small and sustainable through "distributed development" | GamesIndustry.biz

.
Matt Webster, CEO of Fuse Games, is "thrilled" with the critical reception to Star Wars: Galactic Racer, which is currently sitting on a
Metacritic score of 88
for the PS5 version. Speaking to
GamesIndustry.biz
at
Game Republic New Horizons
this week, he says it "felt like we had something good", but you "never really know" how a game will land.
He cautions that it's "too early to tell" whether the game has met sales expectations – "I mean, we're only really through our first weekend" – but he's been pleased to see the audience is receptive to innovation.
Matt Webster  |
Image credit:
Fuse Games
"We felt like we were doing some interesting new things that would be unexpected and surprising, and I think that has helped us," he says, noting that racing games are mired in convention, where it's all about winning. But the roguelike structure of Galactic Racer means that "a really hard fought eighth place finish feels great."
"I was reading
Stephen Totilo's article
about him experiencing the game with his son, and it was his son's first foray into the roguelike structure. And it was really interesting to me because it joined up some thinking around failing in life and coming back stronger. Yes, all games are about fantasy fulfillment and wanting to play around in another world and be successful and learn things. But failing and then learning from that failure and coming back stronger feels like a metaphor for modern life."
Galactic Racer is a great success story for a new UK studio (and a
newly independent UK publisher in Secret Mode
). But the most interesting story is the way the game was made, which, like the game itself, broke away from convention.
The core team working on Star Wars: Galactic Racer was below 75 for most of the game's development  |
Image credit:
Fuse Games/Secret Mode
Traditionally, AAA games have been made by in-house teams of hundreds of people – this week it was revealed that Rockstar now has
more than 4,700 staff members
– but Galactic Racer was made by a core team of 75. In fact, Webster says the core team "averaged a lot smaller than that" through most of development.
Instead of hiring hundreds of team members, Fuse Games has relied heavily on external providers. "What we wanted to do was keep that core small, smaller than perhaps you might have done in the past, and scale capacity and capability with what we call distributed development," says Webster.
"We want to operate at Premier League level," he says. "We know what that takes, but we didn't want to grow and shrink for a bunch of different reasons. Because when you shrink, there's a personal impact to people, but you also lose an incredible amount of knowledge, which I think is probably way more expensive to retrieve."
Three-tier model
What Fuse calls distributed development is split into three tiers, separated in terms of their distance from the core team. Furthest away is traditional outsourcing – involving the creation of art assets, and so on – which typically involves teams in "lower cost locations," Webster says.
"You give a brief, you get an output back, and you integrate it in. Which sounds transactional, but you shouldn't treat it as transactional. It's very important that you build relationships with those folks, you get a better result when you do so."
Galactic Racer was created through distributed development  |
Image credit:
Fuse Games/Secret Mode
Slightly closer to the core team is what Fuse calls external development, which involves giving an outside group a self-contained piece of work. Webster gives the example of Galactic Racer's photo mode, which was handed lock, stock, and barrel to an outside studio.
"It's clear to brief, clear to point to a set of features, and you need a cross-discipline team to bring it together, so you need production, art, UI, and code to create that thing. But because we're in Unreal, it can be self-contained. So someone can go off and build that, and we can slot it in."
"They are, to all intents and purposes, an extension of our team. They just happen to work for another company"
The closest tier to Fuse's core team is co-development. "Those are people that are in our stand-ups, they're in our Slack channels, they're in our code base, they're in all of our team stuff. They are, to all intents and purposes, an extension of our team. They just happen to work for another company."
All of the co-development studios Fuse worked with are based in the UK –
newly Manchester-based
Expression Games recently confirmed it worked on the title – which Webster says was partly about keeping the teams in the same time zone. Working so closely together requires "high-frequency communication", he says, "so time zone makes a difference."
He adds that the UK is extremely well positioned for co-development. "There's just a broad range of experience," he says. "There's different configurations of teams, different cost bases. It used to be in the past that those external studios would help you because they needed to keep the lights on, and really they'd much rather be doing their own thing. And that's changed dramatically."
Now, he says, people are much more willing to work in co-development, partly because games take so long to make these days, and a co-dev role provides much more variety. "They don't want to be on the same thing for three years."
Galactic Racer launched three and a half years after Fuse Games was formed in early 2023  |
Image credit:
Fuse Games/Secret Mode
Webster says that Fuse carefully chose co-dev partners that aligned with the organisation's five values, which he says are "incredibly important" to the company and are "not things that go on a webpage never to be seen again". Those
values
can be summed up as love of games; collaboration; iter
